summary: This document presents requirements and a framework for point-to-multipoint pseudowires over MPLS packet networks. The requirements cover architecture, signaling and maintenance, and are meant as guidelines for developing standard mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7338 sets out what a point-to-multipoint pseudowire must do. A pseudowire carries a Layer 2 or Layer 1 service over an IP or MPLS packet network as if it were a dedicated circuit. The point-to-multipoint version sends one copy of the traffic to many receivers, and the network makes the copies instead of the source. The document lists the requirements for building the tree, attaching receivers, detecting failures and keeping the service running.

subtitle: Extending pseudowires so one stream reaches many receivers without being copied along shared links.

tldr.problem: A provider that wants to deliver Layer 2 traffic from one source to many receivers has to build it out of point-to-point pseudowires, which copies the same traffic once per receiver and wastes bandwidth on shared links.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7338 defines the requirements for a point-to-multipoint pseudowire, a tree of pseudowire endpoints carried over one multipoint tunnel, and lists what a signalling and maintenance design must do: identify the tree, attach and detach leaves, report failures, provide redundancy and scale.
tldr.outcome: The document is a set of requirements, not a protocol. It was written to guide the standardisation of point-to-multipoint pseudowires, which would improve the support for multicast Layer 2 services such as Virtual Private LAN Service and Virtual Private Multicast Service.

facts.value: Unidirectional, Root PE to Leaf PEs

today: RFC 7338 is an Informational RFC published in September 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a set of requirements written to guide later standardisation work, not a protocol an implementer can deploy on its own.

sections.title: The Problem and the Scope
sections.content:
A pseudowire, as defined in the pseudowire architecture of RFC 3985, emulates the essential attributes of a telecommunications service, such as a T1 leased line or Frame Relay, over an IP or MPLS packet switched network. The user perceives a single unshared link or circuit. It carries Layer 1 or Layer 2 traffic, such as Ethernet, time-division multiplexing, ATM and Frame Relay, over a Layer 3 network, and operates edge to edge between the two ends of the pseudowire.

A point-to-multipoint service can be built from a set of point-to-point pseudowires with the traffic replicated at the root provider edge, but that costs bandwidth, because duplicate traffic is carried several times over shared links. This document defines the requirements for a point-to-multipoint pseudowire instead: a mechanism that emulates the attributes of a point-to-multipoint telecommunications service, such as a point-to-multipoint ATM virtual circuit over a packet switched network. The required functions are to encapsulate the service data units arriving at an ingress attachment circuit, carry them across a tunnel to one or more egress attachment circuits, manage their timing and order, and carry out whatever other operations are needed to emulate the service as faithfully as possible.

The scope is the general architecture, a reference model, a mention of data encapsulation, and the requirements for setting up and maintaining the pseudowire. The requirements concentrate on the single-segment pseudowire model; the point-to-multipoint case in the multi-segment model is left for further study, as are packet processing and faithfulness of emulated services, which RFC 3916 covers. Although the document is a requirements specification rather than a protocol specification, its key words are to be interpreted as requirements on any protocol solution designed to meet them.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire makes a packet network look like a dedicated circuit to the customer. Building a one-to-many version out of separate two-ended circuits means sending the same bytes several times over shared links, which wastes capacity. The document asks for a single tree-shaped pseudowire, and then lists what such a design has to get right.

sections.title: The Reference Model
sections.content:
In the pseudowire architecture, both ends of a pseudowire sit at the edge of the same packet switched network and the pseudowire label does not change between the originating and terminating provider edges. This is the single-segment pseudowire, the most fundamental model of the architecture. A point-to-multipoint pseudowire extends it: a root provider edge attached to the source customer edge connects to one or more leaf provider edges, each attached to receiver customer edges. It is also called a PW tree. It is unidirectional, carrying traffic from the root provider edge to the leaf provider edges, and may optionally support a return path.

In this model a single copy of each packet travels over the pseudowire on a point-to-multipoint tunnel, and every leaf receives it because the tunnel itself is point-to-multipoint. The pseudowire should be traffic optimised, meaning only one copy of a packet is sent on any single link along the path. Routers in the core take part in running the tunnel but not in signalling the pseudowires it carries.

The model has to account for three levels of replication: at the ingress provider edge, where traffic is copied to local receiver customer edges; in the core, where a router copies traffic by means of the point-to-multipoint tunnel; and at the egress provider edge, where traffic is copied to local receiver customer edges. It is theoretically possible to skip the core replication and copy everything at ingress into a set of point-to-point tunnels, but that is not preferred, because several tunnels may cross the same physical link and the same packet would then be sent over that link more than once.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic starts at one customer router, crosses a provider edge, travels through the core inside a multipoint tunnel, and comes out at several provider edges, each of which copies it to its own customer. Only one copy crosses each shared link. The copies in the core happen inside the tunnel, not at the source.

sections.title: The Underlying Layer and Multiplexing
sections.content:
The MPLS multicast encapsulation specification defines how MPLS packets are replicated so that a copy is sent to each of several next hops, and that procedure is what a point-to-multipoint tunnel in the packet switched network uses. A point-to-multipoint tunnel corresponds to a point-to-multipoint data link or tunnel, and the pseudowire labels correspond to the top labels of the MPLS packets sent on it. In the single-segment model the pseudowire data unit is replicated by the underlying tunnel, and the pseudowire label is unchanged and hidden from the transit routers.

A solution must support a point-to-multipoint pseudowire over a single point-to-multipoint tunnel, and a single tunnel must be able to carry the traffic of more than one such pseudowire, which is multiplexing. The tunnel may use a different technology, such as MPLS over GRE, or a point-to-multipoint MPLS label switched path, and may be set up with a different protocol, such as the multipoint extensions of LDP or point-to-multipoint RSVP-TE. Which tunnel to use may be fixed by configuration or chosen dynamically.

Multiplexing should be decided by how much the leaves of the pseudowire overlap with the leaves of an existing point-to-multipoint path. Reusing an existing path is attractive because it needs no new configuration, but the routers on that path that are not leaves of the pseudowire would receive traffic they do not want. No special configuration is needed to make them drop it, since they hold no forwarding entries unless they took part in signalling the pseudowire. The operator should decide whether partial multiplexing is acceptable, and a minimum congruency rate may be defined to help; the rate takes into account the overlap between the leaves of the pseudowire and the egress routers of the existing path, where complete overlap gives a rate of 100 percent, and the impact on other traffic sharing the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Several pseudowires can share one multipoint tunnel, which saves the network from carrying a separate tunnel for each one. The catch is that the tunnel usually has more branches than a given pseudowire needs, so the extra branches receive traffic they should not keep. The document says the operator should measure that overlap before sharing a tunnel.

sections.title: Building and Managing the Tree
sections.content:
Two approaches to assigning MPLS labels exist, upstream-assigned and downstream-assigned, but which one to use is left to the solution. The requirements for establishing the pseudowires themselves are that provider edges must be configurable with the pseudowire identifiers and attachment circuits, that a discovery mechanism should let the root provider edge find the leaf provider edges or the other way round, that solutions should allow one-sided operation at the root so that it controls which attachment circuits at the leaves join the tree, and that the root should have a way of learning whether a leaf attached successfully.

On the signalling side, the pseudowire must be uniquely identified, and that identifier must be used in every signalling procedure for it, including setup and monitoring. The root and the leaves must be configured with the same pseudowire type, and on a mismatch a provider edge should refuse the attachment. Interface parameters that describe the capability of an attachment circuit are signalled during setup, so where they apply the solution is required to find out whether the attachment circuit at the leaf can carry the traffic arriving at the root's attachment circuit, and the passive side should be able to reject the attachment if it cannot.

Once the tree exists, a leaf provider edge, or a set of leaves, must be added to or removed from it without any effect on the data and control planes of the remaining leaves. Adding or removing a leaf must also update the underlying tunnel, which may mean adding or removing the same leaf there.
sections.plainLanguage: The tree needs a name that every part of the network uses, and both ends of each attachment must agree on what kind of traffic it carries. The root decides which receivers join, and it must be told when one attaches. After that, a receiver can be added or taken away without disturbing the others.

sections.title: Failures, Protection and Scale
sections.content:
Because the underlying layer has an end-to-end point-to-multipoint topology between the root and the leaves, failure reporting and processing happen only on the edge nodes. A failure event may detach one or more leaves from the tree, and those events must be reported to the root using out-of-band or in-band operations, administration and maintenance messages. The operator must be able to choose out-of-band monitoring, in-band monitoring, or both, and the solution should let the root be informed of leaf failures so that it can update the remaining leaves of the tree.

The solution must provide an in-band status notification mechanism to detect the failure of unidirectional point-to-multipoint traffic, by enhancing existing unicast pseudowire methods such as Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification. When a failure occurs it must report which leaves are affected, by enhancing existing methods such as LDP status notification, and the notification should say whether the fault is in the pseudowire, the attachment circuit or the tunnel. A leaf may also be told about the state of the root's attachment circuit, and the solution must support mapping of operations messages at both ends when a failure is detected on the source side.

Two protection schemes are described. In the first, leaf provider edges are protected by a standby point-to-multipoint pseudowire, with the attachment circuit at the root serving both; the criteria for switching over should be defined, for example that the failure of one or all leaves of the active pseudowire triggers a switchover of the whole pseudowire. In the second, the root provider edge is protected in the same way, with a single attachment circuit at the leaf used to attach the customer to both the primary and the standby pseudowire, and the leaf supporting the mechanisms that select the active one. The document also notes that if the underlying tunnel already provides recovery, the pseudowire layer needs a mechanism to avoid racing between recovery at the tunnel level and recovery at the pseudowire level.

On scale, the solution should grow at worst linearly in message size, memory and processing with the number of leaves. Adding more pseudowires between a root and the same leaves should not make the core routers hold proportionally more forwarding entries, which is achieved by multiplexing the pseudowires onto the tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: When something breaks, the edge routers notice, because only they see the ends of the tree, and they must tell the root which receivers were affected. The root can then update the rest of the tree. The document also describes keeping a standby tree ready and switching to it, and warns that the tunnel and the pseudowire must not both try to recover at the same moment.

sections.title: Security and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The security requirements common to pseudowires, which are set out in Section 11 of RFC 3916, apply, as do the security considerations of RFC 3985. The considerations of RFC 5920 apply to IP/MPLS deployments and those of RFC 6941 to MPLS Transport Profile deployments. Two issues arise from the point-to-multipoint topology itself: the solution should provide means to protect the traffic delivered to receivers, covering integrity, confidentiality and endpoint authentication, and it should support means to protect the pseudowire as a whole against attacks that would cause a denial of service. Safeguard mechanisms should be considered so that an attack on one receiver or on a group of receivers does not damage the whole tree, and both the data plane and the control plane need them.

On compatibility, solutions must be backward compatible with the current pseudowire standards and should use the existing capability advertisement and negotiation procedures for the provider edges that are endpoints. Because operations mechanisms imply advertising capabilities, the solution may advertise point-to-multipoint pseudowire capabilities, and it must not allow a point-to-multipoint pseudowire to be established with provider edges that do not support the functionality; it must have a way to report an error for incompatible endpoints. Finally, where upstream traffic is needed, the solution should allow a return path from the leaf to the root, and the same attachment circuits may be shared between the downstream and upstream directions, so that a customer edge sends traffic back over the same circuit it receives on.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the tree reaches many receivers, one attack can hurt more than one customer, so the design should protect the traffic and keep an attack on a single receiver from affecting the rest. A solution must also stay compatible with the pseudowire standards that already exist, and must refuse to build a tree with equipment that does not support it.

items.title: Detect it
items.text: An in-band status notification finds the failure of the unidirectional traffic.

items.title: Name the leaves
items.text: The report says which leaf provider edges were affected.

items.title: Say what broke
items.text: The fault is in the pseudowire, the attachment circuit or the tunnel.

items.title: Tell the root
items.text: The event reaches the root provider edge by out-of-band or in-band messages.

items.title: Update the tree
items.text: The root adjusts the remaining leaves of the tree.
